newsitem.title: USA: Summit tough on Bosnia, optimistic on world economy.
newsitem.headline: Summit tough on Bosnia, optimistic on world economy.

text.p: The world's leading industrial nations and Russia sent a tough warning to Balkan leaders on Saturday to preserve the faltering peace in Bosnia, but issued an upbeat bulletin on the state of the world economy.

On the second day of an annual summit, the Group of Seven nations and Russia papered over differences on plans to pull American peacekeepers out of Bosnia by mid-1998 and concentrated on telling the former warring parties they could have aid stopped if they let the peace process falter.
They singled out Croatia and Serbia for special criticism, faulting them for failing to demonstrate a stronger commitment to the peace process.

Gathered at a round table at the Denver Public Library, the leaders of the United States, Britain, France, Italy, Germany, Canada, Russia and Japan roamed over a wide agenda although their first problem of the day had a humorous touch -- finding a chair for British Prime Minister Tony Blair.

With Russian President Boris Yeltsin seated at his right, a sign of the prominence Russia is being given at this Group of Seven summit, President Bill Clinton presided over a discussion of what White House spokesman Mike McCurry called "post-Cold War issues" -- international terrorism, drugs, crime and nuclear safety.

In a draft of a statement to be issued later on Saturday, the G7 leaders set out specific economic goals for their countries to ensure that global expansion and a generally rosy economic picture continues.
"We have been encouraged by the many positive indicators in our economies," they said, adding, "But we still have work to do."
Among the encouraging signs: low inflation, reduced budget deficits and solid growth. But unemployment remains high in some countries, particularly among the young, they said.

Setting out specific goals for each nation, the G7 said the United States needed to guard against a resurgence of inflation and balance its federal budget. Japan must rely on domestic demand, not on exports, for faster economic growth.
France, Germany and Italy, all of which are plagued by high unemployment, needed to restructure their economies to promote job creation.
Britain must keep inflation in check and cut its budget deficit further. As for Canada, it has enjoyed faster economic growth recently that should reduce joblessness, the G7 said.

Yeltsin, who hopes for full Russian membership in the G7, was excluded from only one meeting of the day -- a discussion on the world economy. While the G7 talked without him, the Russian was spending the afternoon meeting executives of the Lockheed Martin aerospace and defence company.

In a draft statement to be released later on Saturday on Bosnia, the group -- including Russia -- said, "We are prepared to continue to help the states of this region, but our continued commitment is not unconditional."
A draft copy of the final summit communique to be released on Sunday said Yeltsin's presence "marks a new and deeper participation by Russia in our efforts."

But it stopped short of saying Russia would be admitted as a full member of what would be a Group of Eight as it wants. France says there is a consensus among the leaders to keep Russia out of discussions on international financial issues.

Clinton and Blair, at a private meeting on the sidelines, both agreed that Northern Ireland peace talks could not include Sinn Fein, the political arm of the outlawed Irish Republican Army, unless the IRA agreed to a ceasefire.
Blair told Clinton that Britain had previously promised Sinn Fein it could have a seat at peace talks if the IRA observed a written six-week ceasefire, British officials said.
But they said the IRA response to the dramatic initiative was to murder two policemen in an ambush in Lurgan, southwest of Belfast, on Monday.

Clinton said, "I frankly think now the ball is in Sinn Fein's court. We all have to decide. Everybody has decisions to make in life -- their decision is: are they going to be part of this peace process or not?"

While the presidents and prime ministers spoke, Hillary Rodham Clinton took the leaders' wives by train to a 10,700-foot (3,300-metre) mountain in the Rockies for a lunch and exhibition of square dancing.
Posing for pictures, Mrs Clinton told her colleagues, "Let's do a chorus line" and Aline Chretien, wife of Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, tried to pitch in with a modest can-can.
